prompt.context: Our client, Best Market, is an independent grocer in Manhattan with only one location. The store has been facing increased competition from low-cost competitors and has therefore become increasingly dependent on prepared foods to drive growth. However, the client has reported zero growth in gross profits over the last three years. We have been asked to help the client understand what is causing this lack of growth and what they need to do to turn things around.
prompt.question: What is causing this lack of gross profit growth, and what should Best Market do to turn things around?

clarifying_info.q: Where is the client located in New York?
Does the client have a specific financial target?
clarifying_info.a: No, they just want to identify the problem and figure out ideas to solve it.

clarifying_info.q: Can you tell me more about the client?
clarifying_info.a: The store has been in the community for more than 30 years, is family owned and operated, and is mid-tier — similar to Safeway or Stop and Shop, not Whole Foods.

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's revenues, costs, and profits?
clarifying_info.a: We will get into that later in the case.

exhibits.title: Best Market Financial Summary 2018–2020
exhibits.shows: A table breaking out Revenue, COGS, and implied gross margin for the Grocery department, Prepared Foods department, and the Overall company across 2018, 2019, and 2020. A note states all values are in thousands.

exhibits.title: New Product Cost and Pricing Data
exhibits.shows: A two-panel table with unit economics for Buffalo Chicken Tenders and Made-to-Order Sandwiches, showing price, material cost, prep/labor time, and employee cost per hour.

framework: Best Market (Internal): Financials — review revenue, COGS, and gross margin by segment; analyze product mix and any recent investments
Best Market (Internal): Operations — assess supplier changes and cost structure
Grocery Market (External): Market size and segment growth; consumer taste shifts
Grocery Market (External): Competitive landscape — number, size, and threat level of competitors
Other Considerations: Demographic changes in Harlem neighborhood; NYC health or regulatory restrictions

questions.prompt: Hand the candidate Exhibit 1. What is the root problem as to why gross profits are not growing?
questions.guidance: The candidate should quickly spot that overall revenue is increasing (680→700→760) while gross margin is flat at 220 each year, meaning the profit margin as a percentage of revenue is declining. A strong candidate will analyze each segment: Grocery is stagnant (revenue roughly flat, margin roughly flat). Prepared Foods is the story — revenue is growing rapidly (200→230→280) but COGS are growing even faster (160→190→240), so the segment's gross margin is shrinking. A strong candidate will note they would like to explore both segments but will prioritize Prepared Foods because that is where the margin compression is occurring. The interviewer should then ask the candidate to brainstorm why the Prepared Foods profit margin is declining.

math.setup: Calculate gross margin dollars and margin % by segment for each year.
steps: Prepared Foods gross margin: 2018=40, 2019=40, 2020=40 (flat in dollars). Margin %: 2018=20%, 2019=17.4%, 2020=14.3% (declining sharply).
Overall gross margin stays at 220 while revenue rises from 680 to 760, so overall margin % falls from 32.4% to 28.9%.
math.answer: Overall gross profit is flat at $220K because Grocery is stagnant and Prepared Foods, while growing in revenue, is generating the same absolute gross profit dollars as COGS grow proportionally faster — its margin % is eroding from 20% to 14.3%.

questions.prompt: Hand the candidate Exhibit 2. Best Market introduced two new products in 2018: buffalo chicken tenders and made-to-order sandwiches. What do you think of the economics of each?
questions.guidance: Candidates should calculate profit per order for each product. Most will identify tenders as profitable and sandwiches as loss-making. A strong candidate will flag that buffalo chicken tenders are made in batches in advance and any unsold tenders are discarded at end of day — meaning material cost behaves like a fixed cost, so the store must sell at least 50 out of every 100-piece batch to break even. For sandwiches, the interviewer should note that if asked, it is not possible to simply cut the dedicated labor hours.

math.setup: Calculate unit economics for each product per order/day.
steps: Buffalo Chicken Tenders — Revenue per 10-piece order: $6. Material cost: $0.25 × 10 = $2.50. Fixed cost allocation: 15 min per 100 pieces = 0.25 hrs per 100; at $20/hr that is $5 per batch of 100, or $0.50 per 10-piece order. Profit per order = $6 − $2.50 − $0.50 = $3.00.

Breakeven insight: tenders are pre-made in batches of 100. Full batch material cost = $0.25 × 100 = $25. Full batch labor cost = $5. Total batch cost = $30. Revenue needed to break even = $30; at $6 per 10-piece order that requires selling 5 orders = 50 tenders. If fewer than 50 are sold, the batch loses money.

Made-to-Order Sandwiches — Daily revenue: 40 × $6 = $240. Daily material cost: 40 × $4 = $160. Daily labor cost: 8 hrs × $20 = $160. Daily profit = $240 − $160 − $160 = −$80. Loss per sandwich = −$80 ÷ 40 = −$2 per sandwich.
math.answer: Buffalo chicken tenders earn $3 profit per 10-piece order on paper, but require selling at least 50 of every 100 pre-made tenders to break even given the batch/waste dynamic. Made-to-order sandwiches lose $2 per sandwich ($80/day) because dedicated labor costs alone equal total material costs, and combined they exceed daily revenue.

questions.prompt: What are some ideas to make these two items more profitable?
questions.guidance: If the candidate suggests raising prices, push back by asking how price sensitive these customers are — people grabbing lunch or dinner at a grocery store are likely price-sensitive, making price increases unlikely to work. Evaluate the rationality of other suggestions. Ideas from the casebook are organized below by product.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might the profit margin be declining for the Prepared Foods department?

categories.name: Supplier / Input Costs
ideas: Suppliers have changed, raising input costs
New ingredients required for new products are more expensive

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Prices are not optimized or have not kept pace with cost increases

categories.name: New Products
ideas: New products introduced in 2018 (buffalo chicken tenders and made-to-order sandwiches) have unfavorable unit economics
Product mix has shifted toward lower-margin items

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Waste and spoilage from unsold prepared items
Dedicated station hours not aligned with demand

recommendation: The profitability problem lies with the Prepared Foods department. Two newly introduced items — buffalo chicken tenders (batch waste risk) and made-to-order sandwiches (negative unit economics) — have been dragging down margins. We recommend addressing the unit economics of both products through the actions identified in the brainstorm.
risks: Price-sensitive customer base limits ability to raise prices to cover costs
Reducing labor hours at the sandwich station may not be operationally feasible
Eliminating a product station could disappoint loyal customers and reduce foot traffic
Demand forecasting improvements take time and data to implement effectively
next_steps: For tenders: analyze historical sales data to improve demand forecasting and reduce waste; establish a cut-off time for making new batches; bundle with higher-margin items (chips, cookies, drinks); source cheaper supplies

For sandwiches: cut dedicated station hours to lunch period only to reduce labor cost; consider converting to pre-made sandwiches to eliminate dedicated labor; explore eliminating the station if unit economics cannot be fixed
For both: advertise throughout the store to drive volume and improve capacity utilization; bundle promotions with higher-margin grocery items
Investigate the stagnant Grocery department as a secondary workstream
